name: Face-touching / phone hygiene habit
summary: Wiping phones and washing pillowcases to cut breakouts; untested, low-stakes routine.
lead: The face-touching and phone hygiene habit refers to wiping phones, washing pillowcases and avoiding touching the face in order to reduce breakouts. It is a lifestyle routine discussed in skincare circles.

name: Minimalist routine (gentle cleanser + moisturizer)
summary: Gentle cleanser plus moisturizer; consistent with general dermatology guidance on the barrier.
lead: A minimalist routine strips skincare down to a gentle cleanser and a moisturizer, often to avoid damaging the skin barrier with harsher products.

name: Silicone / onion extract scar gel (Mederma)
summary: OTC onion extract scar gel; trials found it no better than petrolatum.
lead: Mederma is an over-the-counter gel marketed to make scars look softer and less noticeable; its name-giving ingredient is onion bulb extract, and the listed active ingredient is allantoin . Silicone gels and sheets are a related class of topical scar products.

name: Subcision
summary: Needle release of tethered rolling scars; a recognized clinic procedure with mostly small-study evidence.
lead: Subcision is a minor procedure in which a needle is inserted beneath the skin to release fibrous bands tethering a depressed scar, most often rolling acne scars. The term was coined in a 1995 paper describing a tri-beveled hypodermic needle introduced through a puncture .
claims: Subcision works for tethered scars better than microneedling or laser.
It can be done at home.

name: TCA CROSS
summary: Dermatologist-applied pinpoint dabs of high-strength acid into icepick scars; small trials report improvement, with no large controlled evidence.
lead: TCA CROSS, short for chemical reconstruction of skin scars, is a dermatologic technique for atrophic (depressed) acne scars in which a clinician applies a high-concentration trichloroacetic acid (TCA) solution to individual scars rather than to the whole face. It was described by Korean authors in a 2002 report on patients with dark skin types .

name: Punch excision / punch elevation
summary: Surgical removal or lifting of individual deep acne scars with a small punch tool; long established in dermatology, with limited trial-level data.
lead: Punch excision and punch elevation are minor surgical techniques used on atrophic acne scars, particularly deep boxcar scars with sharp edges. In punch excision, a circular punch instrument removes the scar tissue and the defect is closed; in punch elevation, the base of the scar is separated and raised to the level of the surrounding skin .

name: Phenol / Baker-Gordon peel
summary: The deepest classic chemical peel, a phenol and croton oil mixture with documented cardiac and pigment risks, performed under medical supervision.
lead: The phenol or Baker-Gordon peel is a deep chemical peel in which a mixture containing phenol and croton oil is applied to the skin to produce a controlled deep injury, after which the skin regenerates. It is used for coarse wrinkling, sun-damaged skin and some scarring, and sits at the deepest end of chemical peeling .

name: PRP microneedling (vampire facial)
summary: Microneedling with a layer of your own platelet-rich plasma; popular and widely offered, but the added benefit of PRP is described as unproven, and unregulated spas have caused infections.
lead: PRP microneedling, widely marketed as the vampire facial, is a cosmetic procedure that combines microneedling with platelet-rich plasma (PRP), a concentrate of a person's own blood plasma that is rich in platelets. It is offered for skin rejuvenation and acne scarring .
claims: PRP microneedling can clear acne scars within a few sessions
Applying PRP as a cream or serum after treatment improves absorption and results
PRP is a worthwhile hair-loss treatment
PRP can be done at home to save cost

name: Exosome treatments
summary: Stem-cell-derived vesicle serums applied after microneedling; exosome biology is well studied, but cosmetic use is unproven and the FDA treats exosome products as drugs.
lead: Exosome treatments are cosmetic or medical-aesthetic products that use exosomes, small extracellular vesicles of roughly 30 to 150 nanometres released by cells, typically derived from stem cells and applied to the skin, frequently after microneedling . They are marketed for skin rejuvenation, scarring and hair.

name: Picosecond laser (PicoSure/PicoWay)
summary: Ultra-short-pulse laser used for pigment, tattoos and acne scars; small prospective studies report scar improvement, with few large trials.
lead: Picosecond lasers are lasers whose pulses last a trillionth of a second, shorter than earlier nanosecond devices. PicoSure and PicoWay are among the commercial systems clinics use for pigmented lesions, tattoos, skin texture and acne scars. Registered trials cover tattoos, melasma, wrinkles, skin quality and facial laxity .

name: Nd:YAG / Q-switched laser
summary: Nanosecond-pulse laser used by clinics for tattoos and pigment; evidence for appearance uses is mostly small trials.
lead: A Q-switched Nd:YAG laser is a neodymium-doped yttrium aluminium garnet laser that uses Q-switching, an intracavity shutter-like technique, to release stored energy as very short, high-peak-power pulses lasting tens of nanoseconds. In dermatology it is used mainly to treat pigmented lesions and to remove tattoos, and it is discussed in appearance communities as a treatment for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH), melasma and redness.

name: Pulsed dye laser for red scars
summary: Vascular-targeting dye laser used on red scars; trials exist but are small and sources here give no outcomes.
lead: A pulsed dye laser (PDL) is a dye laser, a device whose light comes from a liquid organic dye pumped by a flashlamp or another laser, tuned to wavelengths that haemoglobin absorbs. Dermatologists use it for vascular skin conditions such as port-wine stains and for scars, and it is discussed in appearance circles as a way to fade red (erythematous) scars.

name: Dermabrasion
summary: Surgical sanding of scars, the older standard that lasers largely replaced; sources here mostly small trials.
lead: Dermabrasion is a surgical skin-planing procedure in which a dermatologist or plastic surgeon wears away the upper to mid layers of skin, mainly to reduce acne scars and deep surgical scars. It is distinct from microdermabrasion, a lighter non-invasive exfoliation.

name: Microdermabrasion / HydraFacial
summary: Light exfoliating facials with temporary results; published efficacy data are sparse.
lead: Microdermabrasion is a non-invasive exfoliation that removes the outermost dead skin cells with crystals or a diamond tip combined with suction, usually without anaesthetic. HydraFacial, also called hydradermabrasion, is a branded exfoliative facial that combines cleansing and peeling with suction-based extraction and serum application.

name: Nanofat / autologous fat grafting
summary: Emulsified own-fat injections for scars and skin quality; published work is mostly small clinical series.
lead: Fat transfer, also called fat grafting or lipofilling, moves a person's own fat, usually harvested by liposuction, to another area to correct volume loss or irregularities. Nanofat is a variant in which fat is mechanically emulsified and filtered into a liquid injected through very fine needles, used for scars and skin quality rather than volume.

name: Intralesional steroid / 5-FU for keloids
summary: Clinic-delivered injections of a corticosteroid, sometimes with 5-fluorouracil, to flatten raised keloid scars; a standard dermatology procedure with limited comparative evidence.
lead: Intralesional corticosteroid and 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) injection for keloids is a dermatological procedure in which a clinician injects medication directly into a raised keloid scar to reduce its height, firmness and symptoms such as itch. Triamcinolone acetonide is the corticosteroid most commonly named, and 5-FU is sometimes added or used as an alternative .

name: Scar massage
summary: Manual rubbing or pressure on a healed scar to soften it; widely recommended in clinics, with only weak evidence of benefit.
lead: Scar massage is the manual application of pressure, stretching or circular movement to a scar, typically after the wound has closed, to improve its texture, flexibility and appearance and to relieve symptoms such as tightness and itch .

name: Vitamin E oil / Bio-Oil
summary: Popular over-the-counter scar oils whose scar-fading claims are not supported by reviews of the evidence.
lead: Vitamin E oil is topical tocopherol, a fat-soluble antioxidant applied to the skin, commonly with the aim of improving wound healing and reducing scar tissue. Bio-Oil is a commercial cosmetic oil product marketed for scars and stretch marks; the sources reviewed here do not describe it specifically.

name: Rosehip oil
summary: Natural seed oil promoted for scars and skin; lab and small studies exist but no clear human scar trials were found.
lead: Rosehip oil, or rose seed oil, is a vegetable oil from the seeds of wild roses, usually Rosa rubiginosa (rosa mosqueta), grown in the southern Andes, or Rosa canina . It is used in cosmetics and sold with claims about scars, stretch marks and skin appearance.

name: Lemon juice / baking soda on scars
summary: Kitchen-ingredient scar remedy; no studies found, and citrus juice is a known cause of light-triggered skin reactions.
lead: Applying lemon juice, baking soda or a paste of both to scars is a do-it-yourself practice that circulates as a way to lighten or smooth scars. No clinical studies of the practice were found in the sources reviewed.

name: Pore strips
summary: Adhesive strips that lift surface blackhead plugs from the nose and face; the effect is temporary and there is little clinical research.
lead: Pore strips are adhesive strips applied to the skin, most often the nose, and peeled off to remove the surface of blackheads and sebum plugs. They are a consumer cosmetic product .

name: Pore vacuum
summary: A handheld suction gadget sold to pull blackheads from pores; no clinical trials back or refute it.
lead: A pore vacuum, also sold as a blackhead vacuum or suction blackhead remover, is a handheld electric device that applies suction through a small nozzle held against the skin. Manufacturers market it for drawing sebum and keratin plugs, commonly called blackheads, out of facial pores.

name: Clay mask for pores
summary: Oil-absorbing kaolin or bentonite mask used to make pores look less visible; plausible on oil, untested on pores.
lead: A clay mask is a skin-care product containing mineral clays such as kaolin or bentonite, applied as a paste to the face and rinsed off after drying. Marketing and community discussion commonly present it as a way to absorb surface oil and make pores look smaller.

name: Cold water / ice to close pores
summary: The idea that cold water or ice shrinks pores; no trials have tested it.
lead: The belief that splashing the face with cold water or rubbing ice on it makes pores close or shrink is a long-circulating skin-care idea. Proponents describe pores as opening with warmth and closing with cold.

name: Micropigmentation / scar tattooing
summary: Tattooing pigment into scars to blend them with skin; established in medical use, little formal evidence summarized here.
lead: Micropigmentation, also called permanent makeup or paramedical tattooing, deposits pigment into the skin to reduce the visibility of scars or pigment differences. In looksmaxxing discussions it is raised as a way to blend pale or discolored scars with surrounding skin.

name: Enzyme peel (papaya/pumpkin)
summary: Fruit-enzyme exfoliating mask sold as a gentle peel; a lab study found most tested products had little enzyme activity, and no skin trials exist.
lead: An enzyme peel is a cosmetic exfoliant marketed as a gentler alternative to acid peels. It uses fruit-derived enzymes, most often papain from papaya or enzymes from pumpkin or pineapple, with the stated aim of loosening dead surface skin cells.

name: Tretinoin + microneedling stack
summary: A forum protocol pairing prescription tretinoin with microneedling for scars and texture; each part has evidence, the combination has none found.
lead: The tretinoin plus microneedling stack is a skin-care protocol discussed in appearance forums that combines a topical retinoid (tretinoin) with microneedling, typically with a derma roller, aiming at acne scars, texture and aging signs.

name: Baby Botox / preventative Botox
summary: Small early doses of botulinum toxin to stop lines forming; the idea is popular, and its preventive benefit is untested.
lead: Baby Botox, also called preventative or prophylactic Botox, is a term used in aesthetic medicine and appearance communities for injecting small amounts of botulinum toxin type A into the facial muscles of younger patients who do not yet have deep static wrinkles. The stated aim is to limit the repeated muscle movements that proponents say etch lines such as forehead creases and frown lines into the skin over time.

name: Botox alternatives (Dysport, Xeomin, Jeuveau, Daxxify)
summary: The other prescription botulinum toxins: same basic effect as Botox, different units, onset and approval histories.
lead: Several botulinum toxin type A products compete with Botox (onabotulinumtoxinA) for cosmetic use, mainly treatment of glabellar (frown) lines. They include Dysport (abobotulinumtoxinA, sold in some markets as Azzalure), Xeomin (incobotulinumtoxinA, Bocouture), Jeuveau (prabotulinumtoxinA, Nuceiva), Daxxify (daxibotulinumtoxinA) and Letybo (letibotulinumtoxinA).

name: Topical 'Botox' creams
summary: Peptide creams sold as a needle-free 'Botox' alternative; evidence for wrinkle effects is thin and skin penetration is limited.
lead: Topical 'Botox' creams are cosmetic products marketed as a non-injected alternative to botulinum toxin, usually containing a peptide such as acetyl hexapeptide-8, sold as Argireline. The ingredient is a six-amino-acid fragment of SNAP25, a protein involved in neurotransmitter release that botulinum toxin type A cleaves.
